body:
I was thinking about it this morning and figured a simpler example showing variables in more of the way I use them would do better. This shows that predefined variables with the value set normally work, but how I do it with default values does not work. Similar to the MRP. I also added a before and after for the const variable prints to show that the constants are not being changed, so there is no error there. It is just the argument variable that should be changed.

I know that variables passed and assigned this way are reference changes. Similar to pointers in other code, but I think what I was expecting was the same behavior in all of the types. Where if the argument value was changed then it would just be the new value, instead of trying to adjust the const. And it works for the number and string types just not the others.

```gdscript
extends Control

#Types in 4.x and 3.6
const BLANK_INT :int= 0
const BLANK_FLOAT :float= 0.0
const BLANK_STRING :String= ""
const BLANK_ARRAY :Array= []
const BLANK_DICT :Dictionary= {}

var default_int :int= BLANK_INT
var default_float :float= BLANK_FLOAT
var default_string :String= BLANK_STRING
var default_array :Array= BLANK_ARRAY
var default_dict :Dictionary= BLANK_DICT

var defined_int :int= 0
var defined_float :float= 0.0
var defined_string :String= ""
var defined_array :Array= []
var defined_dict :Dictionary= {}

func _ready() -> void:
	print("test_use with defined vars")
	test_use(
		defined_int,
		defined_float,
		defined_string,
		defined_array,
		defined_dict,
	)
	print()
	print("test_use with default vars")
	test_use(
		default_int,
		default_float,
		default_string,
		default_array,
		default_dict,
	)
	print()

func test_use(
	#Works in 4.x and 3.6
	arg_int :int= BLANK_INT,
	arg_float :float= BLANK_FLOAT,
	arg_string :String= BLANK_STRING,
	#Does not work in 4.x but works in 3.6
	arg_array :Array= BLANK_ARRAY,
	arg_dict :Dictionary= BLANK_DICT
) -> void:
	print("int")
	printt("Before constant",BLANK_INT)
	printt("Before arg",arg_int)
	arg_int = 123
	printt("After constant",BLANK_INT)
	printt("After arg",arg_int)
	print()
	
	print("float")
	printt("Before constant",BLANK_FLOAT)
	printt("Before arg",arg_float)
	arg_float = 123.456
	printt("After constant",BLANK_FLOAT)
	printt("After arg",arg_float)
	print()
	
	print("String")
	printt("Before constant",BLANK_STRING)
	printt("Before arg",arg_string)
	arg_string = "Changed"
	printt("After constant",BLANK_STRING)
	printt("After arg",arg_string)
	print()
	
	print("Array")
	printt("Before constant",BLANK_ARRAY)
	printt("Before arg",arg_array)
	arg_array.append("Changed")
	printt("After constant",BLANK_ARRAY)
	printt("After arg",arg_array)
	print()
	
	print("Dictionary")
	printt("Before constant",BLANK_DICT)
	printt("Before arg",arg_dict)
	arg_dict["Changed"] = 123.456
	printt("After constant",BLANK_DICT)
	printt("After arg",arg_dict)
	print()

```

Thinking about it more, this is probably because of Arrays, Dictionaries, and Objects, being passed by reference instead of value. Not sure if there is a way to just denote reference vs value passing, like other languages do? However for this issue, since it worked in godot 3.6 there probably is a way to do it in 4. Just wanted to mention that since it might be related with this.

Can also repro in 4.6 for arrays even without the custom const definition of empty array as default value (passing direct default value `= []` or nothing for implicit empty default). See #73766 for more details.
